title: Hooked up right: couplings, tug tests and stopping trailer drops
summary: The NHVR has warned that trailers coming off trucks on the road are on the rise, with incidents in 2026 running at double the rate of the same time last year. Most are preventable with a proper coupling check, a tug test and a walk-around before every trip. At Monaro Milk this week is for semi-trailer drivers who couple and uncouple at the fifth wheel, and for every driver, including heavy rigid (HR) tanker drivers, doing a daily check in the dark before an early farm run. HR rigid drivers: the daily check and stopping-the-truck-moving parts apply to you.
key_risk: A semi-trailer that isn't properly coupled at the fifth wheel, or has a worn or damaged fifth wheel or kingpin, comes away from the prime mover: on a highway, on a bend on a rural road, or while you're standing between the prime mover and trailer in a dark yard. NHVR data shows trailer drops and decoupling events are rising, driven by worn or failed coupling parts, driver error or distraction, poor loading and the normal forces a combination puts through the coupling. A dropped trailer can kill other road users who hit it or swerve to miss it, and any truck, rigid or semi, that moves while you're checking or coupling can crush you.
drivers_need_to_know: The NHVR issued a Safety Bulletin in March 2026 because of a clear rise in unplanned trailer drop and decoupling events causing heavy vehicle crashes. In May 2026 it said incidents had doubled on the same time last year, with 8 already recorded in 2026, and 26 recorded between July 2024 and April 2026. The NHVR says many more probably go unreported.
This is happening close to home. In April 2025 there was a fatal crash in NSW when a dolly and two rear trailers came away from the lead trailer.

The NHVR lists four main causes: worn, damaged or out-of-adjustment coupling parts; driver error or distraction (including not following a set coupling procedure); the normal up-and-down, forward-and-back and side forces on a combination, especially where maintenance or fitting isn't good enough; and poor load stability or weight distribution putting extra stress on the coupling.

Semi drivers: before every trip the NHVR expects you to inspect the fifth wheel and kingpin properly, taking off any covers or protective plates to look for wear, damage or defects; make sure the fifth wheel is clean and free of mud and debris that could stop the jaws or lock engaging; check that air lines (susies) and electrical cables are secured and working; walk right around the combination for a final look; and do a tug test before you leave.

Semi drivers, coupling step by step (WorkSafe Queensland): park the prime mover and trailer in a straight line on flat, hard ground. Keep people out of the area. Make sure you have enough light where the fifth wheel is (yard lights, a torch or a work light). Once you've reversed under, check by eye that the jaws have closed and locked on the kingpin, raise the landing legs clear of the ground, do a tug test, wind the legs fully up, connect the airlines (susies) and electrical lines, take one more look at the jaw lock, then do a second tug test in a low forward gear with the trailer brakes on.

Semi drivers: if anything interrupts you while you're coupling (a phone call, the farmer coming over for a chat, a cow on the track), start the whole procedure again from the beginning. Distraction is one of the causes the NHVR names.

All drivers, HR rigid tankers and semis (daily check): the NHVR daily check covers brakes (warning lights, gauges, air tank drains), wheels and tyres (pressure, tread, wheel nuts, leaking hub seals), lights and reflectors, mirrors, windscreen and wipers, body and structure, and fluid leaks; semi drivers add the fifth wheel, kingpin and trailer connections. If you find a fault, write it up and report it before the truck moves. If the vehicle isn't safe, it doesn't go.

All drivers, HR rigid tankers and semis (stopping the truck moving): before you get out of the cab to check or work on anything: engine off, key out, park brake on. Chock the wheels if you're on a slope or doing an inspection. SafeWork NSW says roll-aways have killed several people in NSW, and coupling and uncoupling is one of the times a vehicle can move on you. Semi drivers: never get under or between the prime mover and trailer unless both are fully immobilised.

Semi drivers, dropping a trailer at a farm entrance, a roadside or a depot: pick flat, firm ground, apply the trailer brakes, use chocks where the ground isn't level, and make sure the landing legs are down on solid footing before you release the fifth wheel jaws. WorkSafe Queensland describes a worker knocked under his vehicle while uncoupling on uneven ground, and another whose hand was crushed when a coupling released unexpectedly.
Harvest is starting, so expect more trucks, slow farm machinery and pressure on rural roads over the coming weeks. The NHVR's message is not to rush. A rushed coupling check is how trailers come off.

If you're worried about a coupling, a trailer or pressure to skip checks, tell your supervisor. You can also report safety concerns anonymously to the NHVR's Heavy Vehicle Confidential Reporting Line on 1800 931 785.
supervisors_must_check: We have a written, step-by-step semi-trailer coupling and uncoupling procedure (fifth wheel, kingpin, jaw lock, tug tests, airlines/susies and electrical, landing legs), and every semi driver has been trained and signed off on it for the actual prime movers and trailers they drive.

Daily pre-start checks are actually being done and recorded before every trip by every driver, HR rigid and semi. For semis this includes the coupling items: fifth wheel and mountings secure, kingpin properly engaged in the jaws, air, electrical and ABS/EBS connections attached, and a tug test done.

Every fault a driver reports on a pre-start is followed up: someone is assigned to fix it, it is fixed before the vehicle goes out if it affects safety, and the outcome is recorded. Drivers are never pressured to take a vehicle with a known coupling or brake defect.

Fifth wheel and kingpin inspections and servicing are done by suitably skilled people to the manufacturer's recommendations and the NHVIM V3.2 Section 3 (Couplings) criteria. Workshop checks include fifth wheel mounting bolts and plates, locking mechanisms (jaw lock) and kingpins.

Places where semi drivers couple or drop trailers (depot, farm entrances, changeover points) are flat, firm and lit well enough to see the fifth wheel jaws in the dark. Wheel chocks are on every truck, rigid and prime mover.

Every decoupling event, trailer drop, coupling that didn't lock, or near miss is reported, investigated and written up, and what we learn goes back into maintenance and driver training. This is an NHVR expectation in the March 2026 bulletin.
Run times and schedules leave enough time for a proper pre-start and coupling check, especially on early starts and as harvest traffic builds on rural roads.
discussion_questions: Semi drivers: walk us through exactly how you couple up at 3 am in the yard. Where do you look, and how do you know the jaws have actually locked on the kingpin?

When did you last take the cover off, or get down low with a torch, to check the fifth wheel, jaw lock and kingpin properly (or, for HR rigid drivers, your daily check items)? What would make that easier to do every time?
Where on our runs do we couple, uncouple or drop semi-trailers on ground that isn't flat, firm or well lit? What should we change?
What gets in the way of a full pre-start and tug test: time pressure, weather, darkness, distractions at the farm? How do we fix it?
Has anyone had a coupling that didn't lock, a trailer that moved, or a near miss here or at a previous job? What happened, and was it reported?
practical_checklist: All drivers (HR rigid and semi): engine off, key out, park brake on before you get out to do your checks. Chock the wheels if you're on a slope.
All drivers, daily check: brake warning lights and gauges working, air tanks drained, tyres inflated with good tread, wheel nuts all there and tight, no leaking hub seals.
All drivers: lights, reflectors, mirrors, windscreen, wipers and horn all OK. No fuel, oil, coolant or air leaks.
Semis: remove any covers or plates and look for wear, cracks, damage and loose or missing bolts on the fifth wheel, its mountings and the kingpin.
Semis: fifth wheel clean and free of mud, gravel and old grease build-up that could stop the jaws or lock engaging.
Semis: couple on flat, firm ground in a straight line, with enough light and nobody standing nearby.
Semis: check by eye that the jaws are closed and locked on the kingpin.
Semis: landing legs raised clear, tug test, legs fully up.
Semis: airlines (susies), electrical and ABS/EBS connectors attached and secure.
Semis: final walk-around of the whole combination, then a second tug test in low gear with the trailer brakes on.
Semis: got interrupted while coupling? Start again from the beginning.
All drivers: found a fault? Record it on your pre-start and tell your supervisor before you move. Unsafe means the truck doesn't go.
required_records: Toolbox talk sign-on register for this talk (this app's CSV export, or the printed register).

Completed daily pre-start check for each HR rigid tanker, prime mover and semi-trailer each shift, showing who did it, when, and (for semis) that the fifth wheel coupling was checked and a tug test done.
Defect and fault reports raised by drivers, with the repair, who did it, the date, and when the vehicle was cleared to return to service.
Workshop service and inspection records for fifth wheels, kingpins and jaw locks, including wear measurements.
Written semi-trailer coupling and uncoupling procedure (with version date), and semi driver training and sign-off records.
Incident and near-miss reports for any decoupling, trailer drop, roll-away or coupling that failed to lock, with the investigation findings and corrective actions.
Entries in the Chain of Responsibility breach/exception register for skipped pre-starts, unrepaired defects or schedule pressure, reviewed by the Director monthly.

follow_up_actions.action: Check that our written semi-trailer coupling and uncoupling procedure matches the NHVR March 2026 bulletin and the WorkSafe Queensland steps (jaws visual check, landing legs up, two tug tests, restart if interrupted). Update it if not and re-brief semi drivers.

Check that our pre-start check sheets (HR rigid and semi) include all the relevant NHVR daily check items, and that the semi sheet has the fifth wheel coupling items and a tug-test tick box. Update the sheets if anything is missing.
Get the workshop to inspect and measure all fifth wheels, kingpins and jaw locks against NHVIM V3.2 Section 3, and record the results.
Check that every truck carries wheel chocks and a working torch or work light, and that coupling and drop locations have adequate lighting and firm, level ground.
Review the last 12 months of defect reports and incidents for any coupling, trailer or roll-away issues and confirm each one was closed out.
Put the NHVR trailer drop Safety Bulletin and the Heavy Vehicle Confidential Reporting Line number (1800 931 785) on the depot noticeboard.
Follow up with any driver who raised a coupling, defect, lighting or schedule concern during this talk.
